result:
The universe is under no obligation to make sense to us, yet here we are, stubbornly insisting that it should. We map galaxies we will never visit, decode genomes we barely understand, and argue about the meaning of words that exist only because we invented them. This stubbornness is not a flaw. It is the entire point.

Curiosity is the one human trait that scales without limit. A child asking why the sky is blue and a physicist chasing quantum gravity are engaged in the same activity, differing only in vocabulary and budget. Both refuse to accept “because it is” as a final answer. That refusal has given us antibiotics, spacecraft, and the ability to hold the entire recorded history of our species in a device that fits in a pocket. It has also given us the uncomfortable knowledge that we are a temporary arrangement of atoms on a small rock orbiting an unremarkable star.

I find that last part strangely comforting. If we are not the center of anything, then the pressure to be important disappears. We are free to be interested instead. Interested in the way octopuses solve puzzles, in the mathematics of soap bubbles, in why certain songs make people cry even when the lyrics are nonsense. Interested in the fact that every person you will ever meet is carrying an entire private universe of memories, fears, and half-finished thoughts that no one else will ever fully know.

The best conversations happen when two of those private universes briefly overlap and both people walk away slightly changed. The same is true of ideas. A good idea does not stay owned; it mutates, travels, and comes back wearing someone else’s fingerprints. That is how knowledge actually works: not as a monument we build and then guard, but as a conversation that has been going on for thousands of years and will continue long after we stop talking.

So we keep asking questions. Not because we expect final answers, but because the asking itself is the most interesting thing we do. The universe may never make complete sense. That is fine. We were never promised that it would. We were only given the chance to look around and wonder. That seems like more than enough.
